practice.stem: Eating tamales at Christmas, wearing a yukata (a light cotton kimono) to a summer festival in Japan, and building flat-roofed houses in a dry climate are each an example of a

options.A: culture trait
options.B: culture region
options.C: cultural hearth
options.D: culture complex
options.E: cultural landscape

practice.explanation: A culture trait is one single piece of a culture, like a food, a style of clothing, or a type of building. Your AP course guide lists food preferences, architecture, and land use as culture traits. Each example in the question is one trait. When many related traits go together, that bigger group is called a culture complex.

whyNot.B: A culture region is an area where people share many traits. The question lists single traits, not areas.
whyNot.C: A cultural hearth is the place where a trait or a culture first started.
whyNot.D: A culture complex is a group of related traits that go together. Each example here is just one trait.
whyNot.E: The cultural landscape is what culture looks like on the land. A house fits, but eating tamales is not part of the landscape.

stimulus.title: JOURNAL ENTRIES FROM FIVE STUDENTS ON A SCHOOL TRIP ABROAD (HYPOTHETICAL)
rows: People here eat dinner at 10 p.m. That is just wrong. Dinner should be at 6, like it is at home.
My host family eats dinner late because the afternoon is so hot that people rest at midday. Once I learned why, the schedule made sense to me.
So many restaurants here look like the chains back home. Maybe every place is becoming the same.
I only ate at restaurants that served food from my own country, because the local food seemed strange.
I wrote down the prices of meals here so I can compare them with prices back home.
stimulus.description: A table of five short journal entries written by students during a school trip to another country. Each entry describes the student's reaction to something in the local culture.

practice.stem: Which student's journal entry best demonstrates cultural relativism?

options.A: Student 1
options.B: Student 2
options.C: Student 3
options.D: Student 4
options.E: Student 5

practice.explanation: Cultural relativism means trying to understand another culture on its own terms instead of judging it by the rules of your own culture. Student 2 learned WHY the family eats late (the hot afternoon) and decided the schedule made sense there. Students 1 and 4 do the opposite. They judge the other culture by home-culture standards, which is ethnocentrism.

whyNot.A: Student 1 judges the other culture by home-culture rules. That is ethnocentrism.
whyNot.C: Student 3 notices that places look alike (cultural convergence) but does not try to understand the local culture.
whyNot.D: Student 4 avoids local food because it seems strange. Judging it by home standards is ethnocentrism.
whyNot.E: Student 5 only compares prices. That is a fact-finding task, not an attitude toward cultural differences.

practice.stem: Which of the following is the best example of culture, as geographers use the term?

options.A: Eye color that children inherit from their parents
options.B: A pencil-tapping habit that one student invented and uses before big tests
options.C: The average amount of rain a region receives each year
options.D: A festival song that grandparents teach to their grandchildren
options.E: Blinking automatically when dust blows toward someone's eyes

practice.explanation: Culture is the shared practices, technologies, attitudes, and behaviors that a society passes on. The key ideas are SHARED and LEARNED. A festival song is shared by a community, and grandparents teach it to the next generation. That makes it culture.

whyNot.A: Eye color is passed on through genes. Nobody learns it from their society.
whyNot.B: One person's private habit is not shared by a group, so it is not culture.
whyNot.C: Rainfall is part of the physical environment. It can shape culture, but it is not culture itself.
whyNot.E: Blinking is an automatic body reflex. Nobody has to learn it.

stimulus.title: FIELD NOTES FROM FIVE SITES (HYPOTHETICAL)
rows: Glass office towers built in the 2010s, an international hotel, and coffee shops from chains found in many countries
A brick church built in the 1920s that is now a mosque; the old stained-glass windows remain, and a new sign in Arabic and English hangs over the door
Thick-walled adobe houses with small windows, built by one local family over several generations
A row of new houses, all built in the same style by one company in 2022
A street where most shop signs, restaurants, and festival banners reflect one immigrant group
stimulus.description: A table of field notes describing the buildings and other landscape features a student observed at five different sites.

practice.stem: Which site in the table provides the clearest evidence of sequent occupance?

options.A: Site 1
options.B: Site 2
options.C: Site 3
options.D: Site 4
options.E: Site 5

practice.explanation: Sequent occupance means different groups live in a place one after another, and each group leaves its mark on the landscape. At Site 2, a church built by one group is now a mosque used by a later group, and the old windows are still there. You can see two layers of culture in one building.

whyNot.A: Site 1 shows global, look-alike buildings, not layers left by different groups over time.
whyNot.C: Site 3 shows traditional architecture built by one group, not a series of different groups.
whyNot.D: Site 4 shows new houses from one year and one builder, with no older layer.
whyNot.E: Site 5 shows one group's culture on the landscape, but not one group following another.

practice.stem: In 2019, the climb to the top of Uluru, a huge rock formation in central Australia, was permanently closed. The Anangu, the traditional owners of the land, had long asked visitors not to climb Uluru because of its spiritual importance. This change best illustrates how

options.A: tourism tends to replace traditional land uses once a place becomes famous
options.B: a dry climate can make some landforms too dangerous for visitors
options.C: sequent occupance erases evidence of earlier groups from the landscape
options.D: a national government imposed its own religion on an Indigenous group
options.E: Indigenous beliefs and land rights can shape how a landscape is used

practice.explanation: Uluru is a sacred place for the Anangu, the traditional owners of the land. For years they asked visitors not to climb it, and in 2019 the climb was closed for good. A group's beliefs and its rights to its land changed how the place is used. Your AP course guide says indigenous communities and lands help shape the use of space.

whyNot.A: Here the change went the other way: a tourist activity ended out of respect for a traditional belief.
whyNot.B: Heat and safety were real concerns, but the stem says the closure came after the traditional owners' long request based on the site's spiritual meaning.
whyNot.C: Sequent occupance is about layers left by different groups. Nothing was erased here.
whyNot.D: No religion was imposed. The change respected the Anangu's own beliefs.

practice.stem: Some newer office buildings borrow details from many past styles, such as Greek columns, arches, and bright colors, and combine them in playful new ways. These buildings are best described as examples of

options.A: traditional architecture
options.B: sequent occupance
options.C: postmodern architecture
options.D: an ethnic enclave
options.E: colonial architecture

practice.explanation: Postmodern buildings borrow pieces of older styles, like columns or arches, and mix them in new and often playful ways. They were a reaction against plain glass-box skyscrapers. Your AP course guide lists both traditional and postmodern architecture as parts of the cultural landscape.

whyNot.A: Traditional architecture uses local materials and building styles passed down in one place over generations.
whyNot.B: Sequent occupance is about layers left by different groups over time. The stem describes a building style.
whyNot.D: An ethnic enclave is a neighborhood where one ethnic group is concentrated, not a style of building.
whyNot.E: Colonial architecture follows styles brought by a colonial power, such as Spanish missions in the Americas.

practice.stem: In Country Z, the share of women working in paid jobs rose sharply between 1970 and 2020. Which change in the cultural landscape would most likely go along with this trend?

options.A: More childcare centers near workplaces, transit stops, and neighborhoods
options.B: More stores shifting their busiest hours from evenings and weekends to weekday mornings
options.C: Fewer roads and parking lots, because fewer adults would commute to jobs
options.D: More homes built with large sewing rooms and kitchens for full-time homemakers
options.E: Fewer restaurants and take-out shops, because families would cook more meals at home

practice.explanation: Your AP course guide says attitudes about gender, including women's roles in the workforce, shape how space is used. When more parents of young children work outside the home, families need childcare. So childcare centers open near jobs, transit stops, and homes. That is a change you can see in the landscape.

whyNot.B: With more adults at work on weekdays, busy shopping times tend to move to evenings and weekends, not mornings.
whyNot.C: More people working means more commuting, which usually adds roads, parking, and transit.
whyNot.D: Rooms built for full-time homemakers fit a time when fewer women worked for pay, not more.
whyNot.E: Households where both adults work usually have less time to cook, so demand for restaurants and take-out tends to grow.

practice.stem: After independence in the 1960s, Tanzania's government promoted Swahili as the national language for primary schools and government in a country where more than 100 languages are spoken. Geographers would describe this shared language as

options.A: a centrifugal force, because it divides speakers of different first languages
options.B: an example of relocation diffusion, because it spread mainly through migration
options.C: an example of language extinction, because local languages are no longer spoken
options.D: an example of cultural relativism, because it judges each culture on its own terms
options.E: a centripetal force, because it gives many groups a common identity

practice.explanation: A centripetal force pulls the people of a country together. More than 100 languages are spoken in Tanzania. Giving everyone one shared language for school and government helped people from many groups feel like one nation. Language can also be a centrifugal force when it divides people, as in a country split into language regions.

whyNot.A: A shared national language pulls people together. Language is centrifugal when it divides groups, not when it gives them a common tongue.
whyNot.B: The question is about what the shared language does for the country, not about how it spread.
whyNot.C: Many Tanzanians still speak their local languages too. Swahili was added as a common language.
whyNot.D: Cultural relativism is an attitude toward other cultures, not a language policy.

stimulus.title: LANGUAGE REGIONS OF COUNTRY V (HYPOTHETICAL)

features.name: Region 1
features.sublabel: Most people speak Language A. National capital.

stimulus.description: Country V has three regions. Language A is the only official language, and national schools, courts, and television use only Language A. Most people in Regions 1 and 2 speak Language A at home; most people in Region 3 speak Language B. A zigzag line marks a high mountain range along the border between Region 2 and Region 3.
stimulus.renderNotes: Three side-by-side regions on a water background, each in a different light shade, with name and sublabel. Zigzag line between Regions 2 and 3 = mountains. Square marker in Region 1 = capital.

practice.stem: Based on the map and its description, which outcome is most likely?

options.A: Region 2 will push for independence because the capital is in Region 1.
options.B: The mountains will speed the spread of Language A into Region 3.
options.C: Language will act as a centripetal force that unites Regions 1 and 3.
options.D: Language may become a centrifugal force that pulls Region 3 away.
options.E: Language B will become the lingua franca of Regions 1 and 2.

practice.explanation: A centrifugal force pulls a country apart. Region 3 is cut off by mountains, and most people there speak Language B. But schools, courts, and TV use only Language A. People in Region 3 may feel left out, so language becomes a centrifugal force. Canada, where many French speakers in Quebec have pushed for more self-rule, is a real example of language dividing a country.

whyNot.A: Region 2 shares Language A with the capital region, so language is not dividing it from the rest of the country.
whyNot.B: Mountains are barriers that usually slow diffusion. That is one reason Language B has survived in Region 3.
whyNot.C: Region 3 speaks a different language from Region 1, so language divides them instead of uniting them.
whyNot.E: Regions 1 and 2 already share Language A, so they have no need for Language B as a common language.

practice.stem: Beginning in the 1970s, residents of Barrio Logan, a largely Mexican American neighborhood in San Diego, California, turned land beneath a highway bridge into Chicano Park and painted murals on the bridge's concrete pillars. The murals show Mexican and Mexican American history and culture. This is best described as

options.A: placelessness caused by the spread of global popular culture
options.B: assimilation into a dominant culture
options.C: placemaking that strengthens a sense of place
options.D: stimulus diffusion of an art style from abroad
options.E: ethnocentrism toward other groups

practice.explanation: Placemaking is when people shape a public space so it reflects who they are. The residents of Barrio Logan turned the space under a highway into a park and painted murals about their history. That gives the neighborhood a strong sense of place: a feeling that the place is special and belongs to its community.

whyNot.A: Placelessness is when places lose their uniqueness and look the same. These murals make the place more unique.
whyNot.B: Assimilation means a group gives up its own culture. The murals celebrate it.
whyNot.D: The murals were created by local residents about their own history. The key idea is people shaping their own space.
whyNot.E: Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures as worse than your own. The murals honor the residents' heritage without putting down other groups.

practice.stem: In Nigeria, Islam is the main religion in much of the north, while Christianity is the main religion in much of the south. Which of the following best explains why geographers see this pattern as a possible centrifugal force?

options.A: Islam and Christianity are both ethnic religions, so neither can spread beyond its region.
options.B: When religious differences match regional lines, people may identify more with their region.
options.C: A shared belief in one God makes the two religions a centripetal force across both regions.
options.D: Religious diversity usually leads a state to split into separate countries.
options.E: The pattern resulted from hierarchical diffusion, which spreads religions from capital cities outward.

practice.explanation: A centrifugal force divides a country. In Nigeria, the main religion in much of the north is different from the main religion in much of the south. When religion lines up with region, people may feel closer to their region than to the whole country. Arguments about laws, power, or money can then become both regional and religious, which can pull a state apart.

whyNot.A: Islam and Christianity are universalizing religions that have spread around the world.
whyNot.C: The question asks why the pattern can divide the country. Religious differences that line up with regions tend to divide, not unite.
whyNot.D: Many countries with more than one major religion stay united. Religion becomes a risk mainly when it lines up with other divisions, such as region.
whyNot.E: How the religions spread does not explain why the pattern can divide the country today.

stimulus.title: SPREAD OF RELIGION Q (HYPOTHETICAL)

features.name: Area where most people follow Religion Q by 1500
Area where most people follow Religion Q by 1500 (port town)
Merchants from Land A who settled in the port town in the 1300s

stimulus.description: Religion Q began in the hearth city on Land A. By 1500 it had spread from the hearth city to the villages and towns around it (shaded area on Land A). The arrow shows merchants from Land A who sailed across the sea in the 1300s, settled in a port town on Land B, and built the first Religion Q house of worship there. By 1500 most people in the port town followed Religion Q.
stimulus.renderNotes: Land A on the left, Land B on the right, sea between. Shaded (power) areas: a large area around the hearth city on Land A and a small area around the port town on Land B's west coast. Arrow across the sea from Land A to the port town.

practice.stem: The arrow on the map best illustrates which type of diffusion?

options.A: Contagious expansion diffusion
options.B: Hierarchical expansion diffusion
options.C: Relocation diffusion
options.D: Stimulus expansion diffusion
options.E: Reverse hierarchical diffusion

practice.explanation: Relocation diffusion happens when people MOVE and carry their culture with them to a new place. The merchants sailed across the sea, settled in the port town, and brought their religion along. The religion did not spread through the places in between. It jumped across the sea with the people who moved.

whyNot.A: Contagious diffusion spreads person to person into nearby places, like the shaded area around the hearth city, not across the sea with migrants.
whyNot.B: Hierarchical diffusion moves from powerful people or large places down to smaller ones. The arrow shows people moving.
whyNot.D: Stimulus diffusion is when an idea spreads but changes form. Nothing shows the religion being changed.
whyNot.E: Reverse hierarchical diffusion starts in small or less powerful places and moves up to larger ones.

stimulus.title: YEAR A NEW DANCE STYLE BECAME POPULAR IN EACH PLACE, REGION J (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
stimulus.description: A table listing seven places in Region J with each place's population, its distance in kilometers from the village of Ora, where a new dance style began, and the year the dance became popular there.

practice.stem: Which type of diffusion is best supported by the data in the table?

options.A: Hierarchical, because the dance reached the largest place first
options.B: Relocation, because the dance reached places far from Ora
options.C: Reverse hierarchical, because the dance began in a small village
options.D: Stimulus, because the dance changed its steps as it moved from place to place
options.E: Contagious, because nearby places adopted it first, whatever their size

practice.explanation: Look at distance and year together. The closer a place is to Ora, the sooner it adopted the dance, no matter how many people live there. Tiny Village Q (25 km away) got it in 2001, three years before huge City R (120 km away). Spreading to nearby places first, like a cold passing from person to person, is contagious diffusion.

whyNot.A: City R, the largest place, did not adopt the dance until 2004, after several small villages.
whyNot.B: Relocation needs people to move and carry the trait. A steady spread outward by distance points to contagious expansion instead.
whyNot.C: Village U, the smallest place, adopted the dance last, so the dance did not move from small places up to large ones.
whyNot.D: The table shows only places, distances, and years. It gives no sign that the dance changed.

practice.stem: A U.S.-based burger chain opens restaurants in Country X, where most people do not eat beef for religious reasons. The chain keeps its counters, drive-throughs, and fast service but replaces beef burgers with sandwiches made from spiced potatoes and chicken. This best illustrates

options.A: stimulus diffusion
options.B: relocation diffusion
options.C: contagious diffusion
options.D: reverse hierarchical diffusion
options.E: assimilation

practice.explanation: In stimulus diffusion, the basic idea spreads, but the trait changes to fit the new culture. The fast-food idea (counters, drive-throughs, quick service) spread to Country X. The menu changed to fit local beliefs about food. Same idea, new form.

whyNot.B: Relocation diffusion happens when people move and take their culture with them. Here a business idea spreads and is changed to fit local beliefs.
whyNot.C: Contagious diffusion spreads a trait, unchanged, from person to person into nearby places.
whyNot.D: Reverse hierarchical diffusion moves from small or less powerful places up to larger ones.
whyNot.E: Assimilation is when a group gives up its own culture. The chain kept its basic fast-food model.

practice.stem: A new style of clothing first became popular among teenagers in several small towns in rural Country P. About two years later it appeared in mid-sized cities, and only after that did large stores in the capital city begin selling it. This pattern is best described as

options.A: hierarchical diffusion, because the style moved down from the capital
options.B: contagious diffusion, because the style spread to the nearest towns first
options.C: relocation diffusion, because teenagers moved to cities and took the style
options.D: reverse hierarchical diffusion, because it moved up from small towns
options.E: stimulus diffusion, because each city changed the style to fit local tastes

practice.explanation: Reverse hierarchical diffusion starts at the bottom and moves UP. It begins in small towns or with less powerful groups. Then it climbs to bigger places. Here the style began in small towns. Next it reached mid-sized cities. The capital got it last. Your AP course guide names hierarchical diffusion, which usually moves DOWN from big or powerful places. Reverse hierarchical diffusion climbs the same ladder the other way.

whyNot.A: The style moved UP from small towns to the capital, not down from the capital.
whyNot.B: The style moved up by size, from small towns to mid-sized cities to the capital. Nothing shows it spreading to nearby places first.
whyNot.C: Nothing says teenagers moved. The style spread while people stayed where they were.
whyNot.E: Nothing says the style changed. The same style spread from place to place.

stimulus.title: FOUR LANGUAGES AND THEIR HISTORIES
rows: East Africa, including Kenya and Tanzania
Spread along Indian Ocean coastal trade routes and later inland trade routes; now widely used for trade, schooling, and government among people who speak many different first languages
Formed in the French colony of Saint-Domingue from contact between French and West African languages; now the first language of most Haitians
Brought by French colonization; still an official language after independence
Spoken mainly in its home region; not known to be related to any other living language
stimulus.description: A table describing four languages, where each is widely used today, and how each spread or developed.
stimulus.source: Compiled from standard references on world languages

practice.stem: The role of Swahili described in the table best illustrates which concept?

options.A: Creolization
options.B: Lingua franca
options.C: Language isolate
options.D: Dialect
options.E: Language extinction

practice.explanation: A lingua franca is a "bridge" language. People use it when they do not share a first language. Swahili spread along trade routes. Today, people in East Africa grow up speaking many different languages, but they can all use Swahili to trade, learn, and run the government. Your AP course guide lists lingua franca as one result of the way cultures spread in the past.

whyNot.A: Creolization is when languages mix to form a new first language, as with Haitian Creole in the table.
whyNot.C: A language isolate is not related to any other language, like Basque in the table.
whyNot.D: A dialect is a regional version of one language, like the different ways English is spoken in Texas and in Boston.
whyNot.E: Swahili is growing in use, not disappearing.

practice.stem: Tok Pisin began in the 1800s as a pidgin, a simple contact language used on plantations by workers who spoke many different languages; much of its vocabulary comes from English. Today it is one of the main languages of Papua New Guinea, and many children grow up speaking it as their first language. This change is best described as

options.A: language extinction, because the original trade language disappeared
options.B: stimulus diffusion, because English grammar was copied without changes
options.C: creolization, because a pidgin became the first language of a community
options.D: isolation, because the language developed without contact with other languages
options.E: assimilation, because speakers gave up their first languages for English

practice.explanation: A pidgin is a simple language people create to talk with each other when they do not share a language. When children grow up speaking a pidgin as their first language, it becomes fuller and more complex. It is then called a creole, and the process is creolization. Tok Pisin followed this path.

whyNot.A: The language did not disappear. It grew into a full language that millions of people use today.
whyNot.B: Tok Pisin borrowed many English words but has its own grammar. The key change is a pidgin becoming a first language.
whyNot.D: Tok Pisin formed through contact among many groups, which is the opposite of isolation.
whyNot.E: Tok Pisin is not English, and many of its speakers also speak local languages.

practice.stem: Portuguese is the main language of Brazil, while Spanish is the main language in most other countries of South America. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

options.A: Portugal and Spain divided their colonial claims in South America, and each spread its own language.
options.B: Brazil's tropical climate favored the spread of Portuguese over Spanish.
options.C: Portuguese spread to Brazil through contagious diffusion from neighboring Spanish-speaking countries.
options.D: Brazil's Indigenous peoples spoke languages closely related to Portuguese before 1500.
options.E: Portuguese became Brazil's main language after the country won independence from Spain.

practice.explanation: In 1494, Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, which split their claims to newly reached lands. Portugal's share included eastern South America, which became Brazil. Each colonial power made its own language the language of government, church, and trade. Your AP course guide says colonialism and imperialism helped shape today's cultural patterns.

whyNot.B: Climate does not decide which language people speak. Colonial history does.
whyNot.C: Portuguese did not come from Spanish-speaking neighbors. It came by sea with Portuguese colonizers.
whyNot.D: Indigenous languages of Brazil, such as the Tupi languages, are not related to Portuguese.
whyNot.E: Brazil was a Portuguese colony and became independent from Portugal in 1822.

practice.stem: Most people in Indonesia are Muslim, even though Indonesia lies thousands of kilometers from Islam's hearth on the Arabian Peninsula. Which historical process best explains how Islam first became established in the islands of present-day Indonesia?

options.A: Arab armies conquered the islands and ruled them directly for several centuries.
options.B: Spanish colonizers in the 1500s spread Islam as part of their empire.
options.C: Dutch colonial officials made Islam the official religion of the colony.
options.D: Farmers from India migrated to the islands in large numbers and brought Islam with them.
options.E: Muslim traders on Indian Ocean routes settled in ports, where local rulers adopted Islam.

practice.explanation: Islam spread to the islands of Southeast Asia mostly through TRADE. Muslim merchants sailing the Indian Ocean, including traders from Arabia and from India's coast, settled in busy port towns. Local rulers and traders converted, and the religion spread from the ports to the people around them. Your AP course guide says trade, colonialism, and imperialism helped shape cultural patterns.

whyNot.A: Arab armies never conquered these islands. Islam arrived mainly through trade.
whyNot.B: Spain colonized the nearby Philippines and spread Catholicism, not Islam.
whyNot.C: The Dutch arrived after Islam was already well established, and they did not make it an official religion.
whyNot.D: Islam came mainly with merchants by sea, including traders from India's coast, not with large groups of farmers.

stimulus.title: INDIVIDUALS USING THE INTERNET, SELECTED COUNTRIES AND THE WORLD, 2005 AND 2024
stimulus.description: Grouped bar chart of the percent of each population that used the internet in 2005 and in 2024. United States: 68 and 95. Brazil: 21 and 84. India: 2 and 65. Nigeria: 4 and 41. World: 16 and 71.
stimulus.source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, indicator IT.NET.USER.ZS, "Individuals using the Internet (% of population)," based on International Telecommunication Union data (accessed November 8, 2026). Values rounded to the nearest whole percent.

practice.stem: Which conclusion about the spread of communication technology is best supported by the graph?

options.A: Internet use grew mainly in high-income countries, while lower-income ones changed little.
options.B: By 2024, more than half of the people in each country shown used the internet.
options.C: The gap in internet use between the United States and India widened after 2005.
options.D: Internet use rose in every country shown, but large gaps in access remained in 2024.
options.E: The United States gained the most percentage points because it started highest in 2005.

practice.explanation: Every 2024 bar is taller than its 2005 bar, so far more people can now share music, videos, and ideas instantly. This is time-space convergence at work: places feel closer because communication is faster. But the gaps are still big. In 2024, about 95% of people in the United States used the internet, compared with about 41% in Nigeria.

whyNot.A: India went from about 2% to about 65%, a huge jump for a lower-income country.
whyNot.B: Nigeria was at about 41% in 2024, which is less than half.
whyNot.C: The U.S.–India gap shrank from about 66 points (68 vs. 2) to about 30 points (95 vs. 65).
whyNot.E: The United States gained about 27 points, the smallest gain shown. Brazil and India each gained about 63.

practice.stem: Iceland's language planners often create new Icelandic words for new technologies instead of borrowing English words. For example, the Icelandic word for computer, tölva, was built from older Icelandic words meaning "number" and "prophetess." This practice is best described as an effort to

options.A: create a shared trade language that people in other Nordic countries can easily learn
options.B: resist cultural convergence by keeping the language distinct from English
options.C: speed up the spread of English through relocation diffusion
options.D: turn Icelandic into a creole by mixing it with English
options.E: help immigrants assimilate by replacing Icelandic with English

practice.explanation: Cultural convergence means cultures becoming more alike. One cause is the spread of English and global media. Iceland pushes back. It makes up new Icelandic words instead of borrowing English ones. This keeps the language different and special to Iceland. Your AP course guide says new technology can make cultures more alike (convergence) or more different (divergence).

whyNot.A: New Icelandic words make the language more distinct, not easier for people in other countries to learn.
whyNot.C: The policy does the opposite: it avoids English words.
whyNot.D: A creole forms when languages mix. This policy keeps English words out.
whyNot.E: The policy keeps Icelandic strong instead of replacing it.

practice.stem: A song by a South Korean pop group becomes a worldwide hit through streaming sites and social media. In Country X, fan groups learn the song's dance routine and perform it at local festivals, mixing in steps from a traditional local dance. Which statement best explains this example across scales?

options.A: The song spread mainly by relocation diffusion as Korean migrants moved to Country X.
options.B: The local dance groups show that globalization has little effect at the local scale.
options.C: The example shows convergence at the local scale and divergence at the global scale.
options.D: Time-space convergence slowed the song's spread, so it reached Country X years later.
options.E: Global media spread the song widely, and local groups adapt it to their own culture.

practice.explanation: At the GLOBAL scale, streaming and social media spread the same song almost everywhere, which makes cultures more alike. At the LOCAL scale, fans in Country X mix the song with their own traditional dance and create something new. Geographers look at both scales to see the whole story.

whyNot.A: The song spread through streaming and social media, not because many people moved.
whyNot.B: The fan groups formed because of the global song, so globalization clearly reached the local scale.
whyNot.C: This reverses the scales. The worldwide spread is convergence, while the local mixing adds variety.
whyNot.D: Streaming and social media make ideas spread faster, not slower.

practice.stem: Many young people from rural villages in Country M move to the capital city for school and jobs. In the city, classes, most jobs, and much online content use the national language or English. Over the next few decades, which outcome is most likely for the Indigenous language spoken in their home villages?

options.A: Fewer young people will speak the village language, which may become endangered.
options.B: The village language will become the capital's main lingua franca within a generation.
options.C: The national language will disappear because migrants bring so many languages.
options.D: The village language will spread to other countries through hierarchical diffusion.
options.E: Language use will stay the same, because people keep their first language for life.

practice.explanation: Your AP course guide says urbanization, globalization, and communication technologies change cultural practices. One result can be the loss of indigenous languages. In the city, school, jobs, and the internet all use the national language or English. Over time, young people use their village language less, and their children may never learn it. A language with fewer and fewer young speakers is endangered.

whyNot.B: A small minority language rarely becomes the shared language of a big city. Newcomers usually learn the city's main language.
whyNot.C: The national language is used in schools, jobs, and media, so it grows stronger in the city.
whyNot.D: Moving to the capital does not carry the village language to other countries.
whyNot.E: Children raised in the city often grow up using the city's languages more than the village language.

stimulus.description: A table listing five religions with each religion's hearth, whether it is a universalizing or ethnic religion, and the world regions where most of its followers live today.
stimulus.source: Where followers live: Pew Research Center, "The Global Religious Landscape" (2012; 2010 data). Hearths and types: College Board AP Human Geography course guide and standard references.

practice.stem: Which religion in the table best fits the pattern of an ethnic religion that is still found mainly near its hearth?

options.A: Buddhism
options.B: Christianity
options.C: Hinduism
options.D: Islam
options.E: Judaism

practice.explanation: Ethnic religions are tied to one group of people. They usually do not try to win converts, so they tend to stay near their hearth. Hinduism began in South Asia, and most Hindus still live in India and Nepal. Judaism is also an ethnic religion. But many Jewish communities moved over the centuries, so large communities now live far from the hearth too.

whyNot.A: Buddhism is a universalizing religion, and most Buddhists today live in East and Southeast Asia, far from where it began.
whyNot.B: Christianity is a universalizing religion that is now found on every inhabited continent.
whyNot.D: Islam is a universalizing religion that spread far beyond the Arabian Peninsula.
whyNot.E: Judaism is an ethnic religion, but one of its two largest communities is in the United States, far from its hearth. It spread mainly by relocation diffusion.

practice.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the place names in the table?

options.A: German settlers were the first group to name places in East Texas.
options.B: Spanish place names are found mainly in the Hill Country of central Texas.
options.C: Indigenous place names disappeared from Texas after Spanish colonization.
options.D: Place names record the groups that lived in or settled Texas over time.
options.E: Most Texas place names came from English through contagious diffusion.

practice.explanation: A toponym is a place name. Place names are like a history book written on the map. Nacogdoches comes from a Caddo people. San Antonio and El Paso come from Spanish explorers and settlers. New Braunfels and Fredericksburg come from German immigrants. Each group left its language on the land. Your AP course guide says toponyms can show how languages diffused.

whyNot.A: Nacogdoches, in East Texas, comes from a Caddo people, not from German settlers.
whyNot.B: The German names, not the Spanish ones, are in and near the Hill Country.
whyNot.C: Nacogdoches shows that Indigenous names are still on the map.
whyNot.E: None of the names in the table come from English.

practice.stem: Scholars debate how the Indo-European language family first spread across Europe and South Asia. Which of the following correctly pairs a hypothesis with its explanation?

options.A: Kurgan hypothesis: the family spread with early farmers moving out of Anatolia
options.B: Anatolian hypothesis: the family spread with the diffusion of farming from Anatolia
options.C: Anatolian hypothesis: the family spread with horse-riding herders from the Eurasian steppe
options.D: Kurgan hypothesis: the family spread with traders from the Arabian Peninsula
options.E: Anatolian hypothesis: the family spread from China along the Silk Roads

practice.explanation: Indo-European is the language family with the most speakers today. It includes English, Spanish, Hindi, Russian, and many more. There are two main ideas about how it spread. The Anatolian hypothesis says it spread slowly out of Anatolia (in today's Türkiye) along with farming. That began roughly 8,000 to 9,500 years ago. The Kurgan hypothesis says it spread later, about 5,000 to 6,000 years ago. It came with horse-riding herders from the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian Seas. Scholars still debate the two.

whyNot.A: That swaps the two. The Kurgan hypothesis is about horse-riding herders from the steppe.
whyNot.C: That swaps the two. The Anatolian hypothesis is about farming spreading from Anatolia.
whyNot.D: Neither hypothesis puts the hearth on the Arabian Peninsula. Arabic, spoken there, belongs to a different family (Afro-Asiatic).
whyNot.E: Neither hypothesis puts the hearth in China. Chinese languages belong to a different family (Sino-Tibetan).

practice.stem: Malagasy, the main language of Madagascar, an island off the southeastern coast of Africa, belongs to the Austronesian language family. Its closest relatives are languages spoken on the island of Borneo in Southeast Asia, thousands of kilometers away. Which process best explains this pattern?

options.A: Contagious diffusion through neighboring areas of the African mainland
options.B: Hierarchical diffusion from colonial capitals in Europe
options.C: Stimulus diffusion of an African language that was later rewritten
options.D: Creolization of French and Arabic during the colonial period
options.E: Relocation diffusion by settlers who crossed the Indian Ocean by boat

practice.explanation: Relocation diffusion means people carry their culture when they move. Many centuries ago, people from the Borneo area sailed across the Indian Ocean and settled Madagascar. They brought their language with them, and it jumped over everything in between. That is why a language related to languages of Southeast Asia is spoken off the coast of Africa.

whyNot.A: The nearby African mainland mostly speaks Bantu languages from a different family, so Malagasy did not spread from neighbors.
whyNot.B: Madagascar was a French colony, but French is Indo-European. Colonial rule does not explain an Austronesian language.
whyNot.C: Malagasy did not come from an African language. Its family is centered in Southeast Asia and the Pacific.
whyNot.D: Malagasy is not a mix of French and Arabic. It is related to languages of Borneo.

practice.stem: Which characteristic most helps explain why universalizing religions such as Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism have spread over much larger areas than ethnic religions such as Hinduism and Judaism?

options.A: They are much older than ethnic religions, so they had more time to spread.
options.B: They seek followers from all cultures and actively welcome new converts.
options.C: Their beliefs are closely tied to the land and people of their hearth.
options.D: They spread mainly when their followers migrated, rather than by converting others.
options.E: Their followers are concentrated in the region where the religion began.

practice.explanation: Universalizing religions teach that their message is for everyone. Missionaries, traders, and rulers carried them to new places. They welcomed new believers. Ethnic religions are tied to one group of people. They usually do not seek converts, so they stay closer to home. Your AP course guide says a religion's beliefs and practices affect how far it spreads.

whyNot.A: Hinduism and Judaism are older than Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism, so age does not explain it.
whyNot.C: Strong ties to the land and people of the hearth are more typical of ethnic religions.
whyNot.D: Universalizing religions spread through conversion (expansion diffusion) as well as migration (relocation diffusion).
whyNot.E: That describes ethnic religions, not universalizing ones.

practice.stem: Sikhism began in the Punjab region of South Asia in the late 1400s and early 1500s. Today large Sikh communities, with gurdwaras (Sikh houses of worship), are found in places such as Surrey in Canada, Southall in London, and Yuba City in California. These communities are best explained by

options.A: contagious diffusion from Punjab into neighboring regions of Europe
options.B: hierarchical diffusion, as the faith reached the world's largest cities first and then smaller towns
options.C: relocation diffusion, as Sikhs migrated from Punjab and brought their faith
options.D: stimulus diffusion, as local churches adopted and changed Sikh beliefs
options.E: expansion diffusion, as many local residents in these places converted to Sikhism

practice.explanation: Your AP course guide lists Sikhism as a universalizing religion. It spreads in two ways: expansion and relocation. In these cities, Sikh families who moved from Punjab for work and school built gurdwaras in their new homes. When people move and carry their religion with them, that is relocation diffusion.

whyNot.A: Punjab and Europe are not neighbors. The faith jumped long distances with people who moved.
whyNot.B: The communities formed where Sikh families settled for work, including small Yuba City, not in order of city size.
whyNot.D: Stimulus diffusion means an idea spreads but changes form. Here Sikhs themselves moved and kept their religion.
whyNot.E: The communities grew mainly because Sikh families moved there, not because many local residents converted.

practice.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes acculturation from assimilation?

options.A: Acculturation affects immigrants, while assimilation affects the host society that receives them.
options.B: Acculturation blends two religions into one, while assimilation blends two languages into one.
options.C: Acculturation happens at the global scale, while assimilation happens at the local scale.
options.D: Acculturation adds some new traits; assimilation means giving up most of the original culture.
options.E: Acculturation keeps cultures fully separate, while assimilation lets them coexist as equals.

practice.explanation: Acculturation means you pick up some new traits from the culture around you, like a new language at school. But you keep your own culture too. Assimilation means that over time you take on the new culture so fully that most of your old culture is gone. Think "adding" versus "replacing."

whyNot.A: Both terms usually describe changes in a newcomer or minority group. The difference is how much of the original culture is kept.
whyNot.B: Blending religions is syncretism. Mixing languages into a new one is creolization.
whyNot.C: Both can happen at any scale. Scale is not what separates them.
whyNot.E: Groups living side by side while keeping their own identities is multiculturalism.

stimulus.title: LANGUAGE AND TRADITIONS AMONG FAMILIES FROM COUNTRY F LIVING IN COUNTRY G (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
columns: Speak Country G's main language well (%)
Celebrate Country F's New Year festival (%)
stimulus.description: A table comparing three generations of families from Country F living in Country G: the percent who speak Language F at home, the percent who speak Country G's main language well, and the percent who celebrate Country F's New Year festival.

practice.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?

options.A: The families are moving toward assimilation, but many keep some heritage traditions.
options.B: Most members of the third generation no longer celebrate the New Year festival.
options.C: The data show syncretism, because the families have blended two religions into one.
options.D: The first generation has fully assimilated, since 92 percent of them speak Language F.
options.E: Each generation keeps its heritage language as strongly as the generation before it.

practice.explanation: Read down each column. Speaking Language F at home drops from 92% to 55% to 14%. Speaking Country G's main language well rises to 99%. Losing the home language over the generations is a sign of assimilation. But 52% of the grandchildren still celebrate the festival, so some heritage traditions remain.

whyNot.B: 52% of the third generation still celebrate the festival. That is more than half.
whyNot.C: The table has no data about religion, so it cannot show religions blending.
whyNot.D: Most of the first generation still speaks Language F at home (92%), so it has not assimilated.
whyNot.E: Speaking Language F at home falls in each generation, from 92% to 55% to 14%.

practice.stem: In Mexico, Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) falls on November 1 and 2, the dates of the Catholic holy days of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day. Families build altars with marigolds, candles, food, and photos to honor relatives who have died, customs that many scholars trace to Indigenous Mesoamerican traditions. This celebration best illustrates

options.A: syncretism
options.B: assimilation
options.C: multiculturalism
options.D: ethnocentrism
options.E: relocation diffusion

practice.explanation: Syncretism is the blending of two or more cultural traditions into something new. Many scholars see Day of the Dead as a mix of Catholic holy days, brought by the Spanish, and older Indigenous ways of honoring ancestors. Neither tradition simply replaced the other. They merged.

whyNot.B: Assimilation would mean the older traditions disappeared. Here they survive inside the celebration.
whyNot.C: Multiculturalism means different cultures living side by side while staying separate. Here two traditions blended into one.
whyNot.D: Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own standards. It does not describe this blending.
whyNot.E: Relocation diffusion is spread by people moving. The key idea here is two traditions blending in one place.

exam.title: Unit 3 Practice Exam: Cultural Patterns and Processes
exam.directions: Each of the questions or incomplete statements below is followed by five suggested answers or completions. Select the one that is best in each case. Your score is based only on the number of questions answered correctly, so answer every question. Work quickly without losing accuracy, and come back to any question you skipped if time allows.

questions.stem: Friday-night high school football games, tailgating, marching bands, homecoming mums, and school colors are related traits that together form a

options.A: culture region
options.B: cultural hearth
options.C: culture complex
options.D: culture trait
options.E: cultural landscape

rationales.A: Incorrect. A culture region is an area in which people share particular culture traits; the stem describes a set of related traits, not an area.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A cultural hearth is the place where a culture trait or culture originated.
rationales.C: Correct. A culture complex is a group of related culture traits that together make up a larger cultural activity, such as the practices connected to high school football.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A culture trait is a single attribute of a culture; the stem lists several related traits that function together.
rationales.E: Incorrect. The cultural landscape is the visible imprint of culture on a place, such as a stadium. Tailgating, bands, and school colors together are better described as a complex of related traits.

questions.explanation: One trait is one piece of culture, like wearing school colors. A culture complex is a group of related traits that go together. Football games, tailgating, marching bands, homecoming mums, and school colors all connect to one activity, so together they form a culture complex.

questions.stem: A tourist complains that people in the country she is visiting eat with their hands instead of with forks, and she calls the local way of eating uncivilized. Her attitude is an example of

options.A: ethnocentrism
options.B: cultural relativism
options.C: acculturation
options.D: syncretism
options.E: cultural convergence

rationales.A: Correct. Ethnocentrism is the attitude that one's own culture is superior and the use of one's own cultural standards to judge other cultures.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cultural relativism is the opposite attitude: evaluating a culture's practices on their own terms rather than by an outside standard.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Acculturation is the adoption of some traits of another culture; the tourist rejects the local practice rather than adopting it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Syncretism is the blending of traits from different cultures into a new form.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Cultural convergence is the process by which cultures become more alike through contact.

questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism means judging another culture by your own culture's rules. It means deciding that your way is better. In many cultures, eating with your hands is normal and polite. Calling it "uncivilized" just because it is different from home is ethnocentric.

questions.setLabel: Questions 3–5 refer to the map below.

stimulus.title: SPREAD OF A NEW MUSIC STYLE IN COUNTRY R, 2010–2016 (HYPOTHETICAL)
stimulus.description: Circles show cities and towns in Country R; larger circles mean more people. Each label gives the place's name, its population, and the year the music style first became popular there. The style began in Arlo, the hearth. Fenn is about 120 kilometers from Arlo; Benn and Cora are each more than 450 kilometers from Arlo.
stimulus.renderNotes: One land polygon for Country R on a water background. City circles (island features) sized by population, each with a one-line label underneath. Scale bar bottom left: 100 px = 100 km.

questions.stem: The pattern shown on the map is best described as

options.A: contagious diffusion
options.B: relocation diffusion
options.C: stimulus diffusion
options.D: hierarchical diffusion
options.E: reverse hierarchical diffusion

rationales.A: Incorrect. Contagious diffusion would reach the places nearest the hearth first. Fenn, only about 120 kilometers from Arlo, adopted the style in 2015, years after much more distant large cities.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Relocation diffusion occurs when people migrate and carry a trait with them; the map shows adoption in place, in order of city size.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stimulus diffusion involves an underlying idea spreading while the trait itself is changed; the map gives no evidence that the style changed.
rationales.D: Correct. The style spread from the largest city to other large cities, then to medium-sized cities, and last to small towns, regardless of distance from the hearth. Spread down an urban hierarchy is hierarchical diffusion.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Reverse hierarchical diffusion moves from small places up to larger ones; here the smallest places adopted the style last.

questions.explanation: Follow the years. Arlo, the biggest city, had it in 2010. The big cities Benn and Cora got it in 2011. The medium cities Dell and Eskar got it in 2013. The small towns Fenn and Gale got it last, in 2015 and 2016. The style moved down the ladder of city size, not outward by distance. That is hierarchical diffusion.

questions.stem: Fenn is the place closest to Arlo, yet it was one of the last places to adopt the music style. Which of the following best explains this?

options.A: Distance decay means places nearest a hearth tend to be the last to adopt a trait.
options.B: The style reached Fenn when people from Arlo moved there, through relocation diffusion.
options.C: New trends often move first between big, well-connected cities, then down to small towns.
options.D: Fenn's small population places it in a different culture region from the rest of Country R.
options.E: Contagious diffusion spreads a trait to the largest places first and the closest places last.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Distance decay means interaction declines as distance increases, so nearby places usually adopt a trait sooner, not later.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The map gives no evidence of migration, and relocation diffusion would not explain why a nearby town adopted the style later than distant large cities.
rationales.C: Correct. In hierarchical diffusion, a trait moves first among the largest and most connected places, through media, business, and travel links, and reaches small towns later, even towns close to the hearth.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nothing on the map suggests Fenn belongs to a different culture region; Fenn and Gale, the two smallest places, both adopted the style last, which reflects their size.
rationales.E: Incorrect. This misdefines contagious diffusion, which spreads to the nearest people and places first regardless of size.

questions.explanation: Big cities are tied to each other by media companies, concert tours, airports, and lots of travelers. So a new trend jumps from one big city to another first. Small towns get it later, even if they are close by. That is why little Fenn waited until 2015.

questions.stem: Suppose the same music style had first appeared in Arlo in 2024, when nearly everyone in Country R used streaming services and social media. Compared with the map, the spread would most likely have been

options.A: slower, because online media make distance decay stronger
options.B: limited mainly to large cities, because small towns lack media companies
options.C: about the same, because trends would still move down the urban hierarchy year by year
options.D: carried mainly by migrants, making relocation diffusion the main process
options.E: faster and less tied to city size, because of time-space convergence

rationales.A: Incorrect. Online media weaken the effect of distance on interaction; they do not strengthen distance decay.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Listeners do not need local media companies to stream music; anyone with internet access can hear a new style, wherever they live.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The AP course framework notes that communication technologies such as the internet are reshaping and accelerating interactions among people, so the slow, year-by-year movement down the urban hierarchy shown on the map would be much less likely.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Online sharing spreads a trait without people moving, so relocation diffusion would not become the main process.
rationales.E: Correct. Time-space convergence, the shrinking of the time it takes for people and ideas to travel between places, means people in small towns can hear a new style online at nearly the same time as people in big cities. Adoption would be faster and depend less on the urban hierarchy.

questions.explanation: With streaming and social media, a song posted in Arlo can be heard in tiny Fenn the same day. Distance and city size matter much less. That is time-space convergence: new technology makes places feel closer together, so trends spread faster and more evenly.

questions.stem: In the early 1800s, Sequoyah, a Cherokee man who did not read English, saw that English speakers could communicate through writing. He then created a new writing system, with a symbol for each syllable of the Cherokee language, which he completed in 1821. This is an example of

options.A: stimulus diffusion
options.B: relocation diffusion
options.C: contagious diffusion
options.D: hierarchical diffusion
options.E: assimilation

rationales.A: Correct. In stimulus diffusion, an underlying idea spreads, but the trait itself is changed or reinvented by the receiving culture. The idea of writing spread, and Sequoyah created a new system for the Cherokee language rather than adopting English writing.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Relocation diffusion occurs when people migrate and carry culture with them; Sequoyah adapted an idea he encountered rather than receiving a trait carried by migrants.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Contagious diffusion spreads a trait, unchanged, from person to person; here the trait was reinvented.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Hierarchical diffusion moves from people or places of high rank down the hierarchy; the key feature here is the transformation of the idea.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Assimilation would mean giving up Cherokee culture; the syllabary was created to write the Cherokee language.

questions.explanation: Stimulus diffusion means the IDEA spreads, but people change it to fit their own culture. Sequoyah got the idea of writing from seeing English, but he made a brand-new writing system for Cherokee.

questions.stem: International rules require pilots and air traffic controllers on international flights to be able to communicate in English, even when neither the pilot nor the controller speaks English as a first language. English in this role is best described as

options.A: a creole
options.B: a lingua franca
options.C: a dialect
options.D: a language isolate
options.E: a pidgin

rationales.A: Incorrect. A creole develops when a pidgin becomes the first language of a community; aviation English did not develop that way.
rationales.B: Correct. A lingua franca is a language used for communication among people who do not share a first language. English plays this role in international aviation, as well as in much of international business and science.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A dialect is a regional or social variety of a language.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A language isolate has no known relationship to other languages, as with Basque; English belongs to the Germanic branch of the Indo-European family.
rationales.E: Incorrect. A pidgin is a simplified mixture of languages created for limited contact; aviation uses standard English with set phrases, not a new mixed language.

questions.explanation: A lingua franca is a "bridge" language that people use when they do not share a first language. A pilot from Brazil and a controller in Japan can both use English to talk. English is the lingua franca of the skies.

questions.stem: Portuguese is an official language in Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, and Timor-Leste, countries on three different continents. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

options.A: Portuguese spread by contagious diffusion from Brazil to Africa and then to Asia.
options.B: The four countries share a tropical climate that favored the spread of Portuguese.
options.C: Portuguese formed as a pidgin among traders in Africa and later spread to Europe.
options.D: Large numbers of Portuguese workers moved to these countries in the last 20 years.
options.E: Portugal colonized these places, and its language remained after independence.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Contagious diffusion spreads to nearby places; these countries are separated by oceans, and Portuguese reached each one by sea from Portugal.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Climate does not determine language; the pattern reflects colonial history, not environmental conditions.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Portuguese is a Romance language that developed in Europe from Latin; it did not begin as an African trade pidgin.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Portuguese has been used in these places for centuries, far longer than recent migration could explain.
rationales.E: Correct. Portugal built a colonial and trading empire beginning in the 1400s and 1500s. Colonial rule spread Portuguese as the language of government, schooling, and trade, and the former colonies kept it as an official language after independence.

questions.explanation: These countries are far apart, but they were all once Portuguese colonies. The colonizers made Portuguese the language of government, schools, and business. After independence, Portuguese stayed. Your AP course guide says colonialism and imperialism helped shape the cultural patterns we see today.

questions.stem: Haitian Creole developed in the 1600s and 1700s in the French colony of Saint-Domingue (present-day Haiti). Most of its vocabulary comes from French, while much of its grammar reflects West African languages spoken by enslaved Africans brought to the colony. Today it is the native language of most Haitians. The development of Haitian Creole best illustrates

options.A: language extinction caused by the spread of a colonial language
options.B: creolization resulting from contact between cultures under colonialism
options.C: the diffusion of an Indo-European language by contagious expansion
options.D: stimulus diffusion of the idea of writing from West Africa to Europe
options.E: the formation of a dialect through isolation from other languages

rationales.A: Incorrect. Haitian Creole did not disappear; it became the native language of most Haitians and, since 1987, an official language of Haiti alongside French.
rationales.B: Correct. Creolization is the blending of cultural elements, including languages, into new forms. Under French colonial rule, contact between French and West African languages produced a new language that children learned as their first language.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Haitian Creole formed through intense contact among groups within one colony, not through the gradual spread of French into neighboring areas.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The stem describes a new spoken language forming, not the spread of the idea of writing.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Haitian Creole formed through contact among speakers of different languages, the opposite of isolation.

questions.explanation: Creolization happens when cultures come into close contact and mix to make something new. In colonial Haiti, French and West African languages mixed. Children grew up speaking the mix as their first language, and a new language, Haitian Creole, was born.
